title: Broken Ergodicity and the Violation of the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem Lead to Generalization Beyond Overfitting in Machine Learning
abstract: The remarkable ability of modern neural networks to generalize improves with increasing network capacity, even when the number of model parameters or effective degrees of freedom exceeds the number of training data points. This phenomenon is all the more surprising given that generalization error diverges when the number of model parameters approaches a critical value from below. Here we use dynamical mean field theory to show that this so-called "double descent" behavior is the outcome of a phase transition in the stochastic field theory describing the training process. We calculate the critical exponents and scaling function of the double descent phase transition, and show that it is marked by a breakdown of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem associated with broken ergodicity. The corresponding response function has the same functional form as the simple London model of the superconducting transition, with the rigidity of the wave function corresponding to the neural network's ability to generalize accurately.
summary: This work explains the counterintuitive 'double descent' in overparameterized neural networks by framing it as a dynamical phase transition. The key diagnostic tool is the breakdown of the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem (FDT). This mechanism links successful generalization to concepts from condensed matter physics, specifically those governing superconducting transitions.
main_problem: The paper addresses the 'double descent' phenomenon in overparameterized neural networks, seeking a physical mechanism beyond classical bias-variance trade-offs.
main_result: This generalization behavior is shown to be the outcome of a dynamical phase transition marked by the breakdown of the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem (FDT) and associated with broken ergodicity.
method: The analysis employs Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) applied to the stochastic gradient flow describing network training dynamics in the thermodynamic limit.
model_or_system: The system models single-layer linear regression trained via SGD, analyzed by mapping its dynamics onto an effective stochastic process analogous to superconducting phase transitions.
key_observables: Generalization error ($\epsilon_g$), training error ($\epsilon_t$), Response function $R(t, t')$, and the violation of the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem (FDT).
important_parameters: The complexity parameter $\alpha = d/N$, which dictates the regime: underparameterized ($\alpha < 1$), interpolation threshold ($\alpha = 1$), and overparameterized ($\alpha > 1$).
main_assumptions: The use of DMFT approximations, assuming a saddle-point approximation for the dynamical generating functional, and drawing analogies to established condensed matter models like the London model.
figures_summary: Not specified in notes; figures likely illustrate the divergence/convergence of generalization error across different $\alpha$ regimes and the mathematical forms of correlation functions before and after FDT violation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the ML problem (double descent), then applying DMFT to derive the effective dynamics, identifying the FDT breakdown as the key diagnostic for a dynamical phase transition, and finally drawing precise analogies between this transition and superconductivity/London models.
why_interesting: It provides a deep theoretical link between non-equilibrium statistical physics concepts (ergodicity breaking, FDT violation) and modern machine learning phenomena, suggesting that generalization is governed by underlying physical principles of ordered phases.
